questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A year of applications
questions.learningObjective: Explain why one calendar year of membership applications was remarkable.
questions.stem: The planner's memorandum opens with a table of membership applications filed in a single calendar year; why is that year remembered as remarkable?

options.text: Seventeen new states in one region gained independence that year and each applied for membership.
Every region of the world applied for membership within the same twelve months.
options.misconception: invents simultaneous applications from every region

options.text: Membership in that year was decided without any vote by the general assembly at all.
That year the organisation permanently lowered its rules for admitting new members.
options.misconception: claims admission rules were permanently lowered

questions.explanation: The table lists seventeen applications from newly independent states in one region, the largest single-year rush of membership. Each still needed a council recommendation and an assembly vote, so no rule was bypassed.
questions.hint: Count the entries in the table.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A circular that set the timetable
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a published circular could set the timetable for decolonisation.
questions.stem: In the second appendix, the planner copies a circular issued by a colonial power; explain how one document could set the timetable for decolonisation.

answer.exemplar: The circular converted an open-ended imperial claim into a dated programme. It told administrators and local leaders when self-government would begin, when elections would be held and which powers would be retained at the end of the transition. That announcement mattered because a colonial power's word was the thing every negotiated settlement waited for: once a date was published, local parties could plan around it, and competing powers could no longer offer a rival timetable. Decolonisation then acquired a schedule, and negotiations became about terms rather than about whether independence would come.

questions.explanation: A circular published a schedule that local parties and rival powers could plan around, replacing vague promises with dates. Once it was public, talks were about terms, not about whether independence would come.
questions.hint: A published date changes what negotiation is about.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Borders drawn before a colony existed
questions.learningObjective: Explain what followed from borders being fixed before any administration existed.

stimulus.body: A note records that a nineteenth-century conference of European powers divided a continent between themselves in writing, drawing many of the lines along meridians and parallels through regions where no European administration yet existed. The note adds that the conference created no governments and no territories, only claims.

questions.stem: A note appended to the memorandum records that the borders were fixed before any administration existed; what did that order of events make possible?

options.text: It meant that no local population was consulted about the lines that later became its borders.
options.misconception: invents a consultation that never happened

options.text: It meant that the borders could be adjusted at will whenever the peoples concerned asked.
It meant that the powers concerned had already built roads and administrations along the lines.
It meant that the lines were drawn for the convenience of outsiders, not for the people living there.

questions.explanation: Because the lines were made on paper before any administration existed, they served the claims of the powers drawing them, not the communities crossed. Independence later inherited that geometry.
questions.hint: Ask who the lines were drawn to serve.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The contest for the centre
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the contest over the central state was so damaging.

stimulus.body: A file on the central state records that within months of independence its richest southern province declared itself separate and appealed for outside support, that the central government appealed to the organisation for help, and that a force organised by member states was sent while several members supplied arms to the province as well.

questions.stem: The memo's section on the contested centre explains that the crisis was so damaging because what?

options.text: The province's economy produced almost all of the young state's revenue.
The neighbouring colonial power refused to accept the new state's independence.
options.misconception: makes the crisis a matter of recognition only

options.text: The dispute was fought with foreign support on both sides, inside one new state.
The organisation ruled that the province's separation was lawful and binding on all members.

questions.explanation: Foreign backing on both sides of a fight inside one new state made the centre a prize of the wider rivalry. The organisation was drawn in because it could offer a force that was not a foreign army.
questions.hint: Look for foreign support on both sides.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A third option in choosing alliances
questions.learningObjective: Summarise what the third option in choosing alliances actually was.
questions.stem: The applicant's file, quoted in the memo, asks whether joining a bloc was the only choice; which summary of the third option is accurate?

options.text: It was a loose group of states that sought military protection from a single leader.
options.misconception: describes an alliance rather than non-alignment

options.text: It was a movement that required members to reject economic cooperation with the western powers.
It was a movement of states that refused to join either bloc while co-operating with both.
It was an organisation that replaced the two blocs in the council of the organisation.
options.misconception: claims it displaced the permanent members

questions.explanation: The third option was organised independence: states declined to join either bloc and refused alignments while seeking a voice in decisions affecting them. It was a position within the system, not a rival bloc.
questions.hint: Think about refusing alignment without refusing cooperation.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A declaration that refused the blocs
questions.learningObjective: Explain how refusing to choose sides protected the states that made the declaration.
questions.stem: Reading the memo's discussion of the declaration, one finds a list of refusals; explain how refusing to choose sides protected the states that made it.

answer.exemplar: A declaration of refusal worked because it turned neutrality into a positive position. By rejecting military alliances, foreign bases and the pressure to take sides, the states signing it removed the expectation that each would be available to one camp or the other. Their protection came from being useful to both: aid and trade flowed from the west while relations with the east were kept warm. The declaration also stated principles of peaceful coexistence, which gave partners of either camp a respectable vocabulary for working with them without appearing to defect.

questions.explanation: By refusing alignments and bases, the signatories removed the expectation that they were available to either camp, which made them useful to both. Non-alignment became a positive position rather than an absence.
questions.hint: Ask what each camp gained from a non-aligned state.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Writing down how a new state is organised
questions.learningObjective: Identify the kind of political order defined by a new state's constitution.

stimulus.body: A file describes the constitution adopted by a newly independent state. It provides for a single chamber elected by universal adult suffrage, a ceremonial head of state chosen by parliament, and a prime minister holding the real executive power. It also states that the constitution may be amended only by a two-thirds majority of the elected members.

questions.stem: The memorandum's file on constitutions says that this arrangement gave the new state what kind of political order?

options.text: A presidency with a fixed term, insulated from the elected majority by the constitution.
A military council that suspended the constitution within two years of independence.
A monarchy whose succession was settled by the constitution alone.
A parliamentary system in which the executive answers to the elected chamber.

questions.explanation: A ceremonial presidency, an elected chamber and a prime minister holding executive power make the parliamentary pattern, where the government depends on the chamber's confidence. A fixed presidency would look quite different.
questions.hint: Ask who holds the real executive power.

questions.topic: Redrawing internal boundaries
questions.learningObjective: Explain why inherited internal borders mattered after independence.

questions.stem: A later memo, filed with the same city, notes that the inherited internal borders mattered most because what?

options.text: They matched the districts the colonial administration had used to move goods.
options.misconception: reduces the issue to trade routes

options.text: They were so precise that no group could claim to have been misplaced by them.
options.misconception: claims the units were always accurate

options.text: They were drawn by the independent government to correct colonial mistakes.
options.misconception: attributes the borders to the new government

options.text: They fixed the boundaries of the regions into which political competition was organised.

questions.explanation: Because the old provinces became the units of regional power, lines drawn on paper by outsiders came to decide which communities shared a voice in the new state. Cartography turned into a matter of domestic politics.
questions.hint: Ask what the regions controlled.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The contest for the centre
questions.learningObjective: Explain how the crisis shaped the new central state.
questions.stem: The memo's closing section on the centre states that the contest was decided in ways the constitution did not anticipate; explain how that shaped the new state.

answer.exemplar: The constitution gave the new state a united territory and a single authority over it, and then the dispute showed how thin that authority was. Because the seceding province was rich, mineral rich and had supporters abroad, the central government could not simply suppress it, and the presence of a foreign-backed force on its own border made the contest unmanageable by decree. The state that emerged therefore began with a very strong centre in law and a very weak one in practice, which is why its early politics turned on who could command force rather than on who had a claim to the office.

questions.explanation: The crisis exposed how little the new state's authority amounted to when a wealthy province had external backing. The result was a state strong in law and weak in practice, with politics turned to force.
questions.hint: Compare the constitution's claims with the actual power.

questions.explanation: The rule about staging points stopped a member's territory becoming a launchpad for a bloc's campaign, which kept alignment reversible. Cooperation remained permitted, so the refusal was narrow and deliberate.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A year of applications
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a single year's rush of applications changed the organisation's practice.
questions.stem: The planner counts in the opening table that seventeen states applied in one year; explain what that volume did to the organisation's practice.

answer.exemplar: A rush of seventeen applications forced the organisation to change how it received new members. Instead of treating each admission as a separate political occasion, it began to move several together, granting membership in a single day after one round of votes, which spared the delegations repeated flights and speeches. Administratively, the surge also meant that the small professional staff could no longer vet each candidate individually, so standard criteria and a settled routine had to carry the weight. The practical effect was that the organisation's capacity was tested and, in the end, expanded.

questions.explanation: Seventeen applications at once obliged the organisation to process admissions together in a single session rather than one at a time. That produced a routine which made the next surge easier to absorb.
questions.hint: Think about how the handling of cases changed.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A declaration that refused the blocs
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a written set of principles mattered to states that refused to choose sides.
questions.stem: The planner's table on the declaration shows that the principles were written to be usable; explain why a written set of principles mattered to states that had refused to choose sides.

answer.exemplar: Written principles converted a refusal into a position that could be defended and repeated. A state could point to a text that said it would not host bases, would not support the domination of a region, and would not be drawn into the rivalry, and it could do so in its own words rather than in the language of either camp. That mattered in practice, because other governments and movements frequently tested the commitment by asking for a base, a vote or a signature. A text could be cited, compared with earlier declarations and used to settle a dispute internally without reopening the whole question of alignment.

questions.explanation: Written principles gave the refusal a citable form states could invoke when a camp asked for a base, a vote or a signature. That turned a position vulnerable to pressure into one defended with words on record.
questions.hint: Think about how a text is used under pressure.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Borders drawn before a colony existed
questions.learningObjective: Explain why new states adopted borders drawn by outsiders.
questions.stem: The planner's summary of the border partition notes that the lines were later adopted by newly independent states; explain why that was not a simple act of convenience.

answer.exemplar: Adopting the old lines was never merely convenient, because it settled questions that the new states had no other means to settle. Each government had to produce a defensible frontier, and the inherited line was the only one that any neighbouring government could also be expected to accept. There was no survey, no population register and no shared authority to appeal to, so a line drawn by outsiders had become the one piece of shared administrative fact available. Accepting it avoided an immediate crisis at the moment of independence, at the price of locking in divisions that later had to be corrected from inside.

questions.explanation: The inherited line was the only frontier each new government could expect its neighbours to accept, so adopting it settled the border rather than saving effort. Its cost was locking in internal divisions.
questions.hint: Think about what each government needed from its neighbour.

questions.topic: The contest for the centre

stimulus.body: An aftermath note records that the central government was unable to hold the seceding province without outside troops, that the outside force did not stay long once the fighting stopped, and that the province was admitted to the organisation's own assemblies as a part of the state rather than as a separate member.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why a third position could be sustained where a formal alliance could not.

answer.exemplar: A formal alliance is a standing commitment to fight another's war, and states that resented such a commitment found it hard to sustain once a crisis actually arrived. The third position avoided the obligation entirely by refusing bases and alignments while continuing to trade and to receive aid from all sides, so no one's defence was entangled with another's quarrel. It also had a moral argument at hand, in the form of a commitment to peaceful coexistence, which gave states a respectable way to decline pressure from either camp without appearing to prefer the other.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A circular that set the timetable
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the timetable mattered most to those seeking self-government.
questions.stem: The planner's note on the circular argues that the timetable mattered most to the leaders of the movements seeking self-government; explain why.

answer.exemplar: The published timetable changed what the local leaders had to prove. Until a colonial power announced a schedule, the argument had to be that independence was inevitable and that any refusal was a moral failure. Once stages and dates were on paper, the leaders could shift to a narrower and much stronger claim: that the colonial power had itself set the standard by announcing a process, and that its failure to meet the dates it had published was a breach of its own undertaking. The timetable therefore converted an argument about justice into an argument about performance, which is far easier to sustain in negotiation and far harder for a colonial government to answer.

questions.explanation: A published schedule let local leaders shift from arguing that independence was inevitable to pointing out that the colonial power had missed its own announced dates. That changed the argument from justice to performance.
questions.hint: Think about who set the standard.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Writing down how a new state is organised
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the method of adopting a constitution mattered to a young state.
questions.stem: The memorandum's appendix on the constitutions describes how the text was adopted; explain why the method of adoption mattered to a young state.

answer.exemplar: The method of adoption decided who owned the new order. A text imposed by a departing colonial government, however reasonable its contents, could be dismissed by the public as someone else's document, and every subsequent dispute could be framed as a contest over the original settlement. If the text was made by representatives the people themselves had chosen, and then confirmed in public, it became the thing the majority had agreed to, and disputes shifted from the ground of the settlement itself to the ground of the institutions it created. For a young state that needed to settle who had the right to command, that difference in legitimacy was worth as much as any clause in the text.

questions.explanation: A text made by elected representatives and confirmed publicly became the people's own settlement, so later disputes turned on institutions, not the original bargain. An imposed text could be dismissed as foreign.
questions.hint: Think about who could claim the text.

questions.hint: Count the units before and after.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A year of applications
questions.learningObjective: Explain the consequences of a year of applications for the organisation's agenda.
questions.stem: According to the memo's timetable, the year of the rush carried consequences for the organisation's own agenda; explain what they were.

answer.exemplar: An influx of seventeen new members changed the arithmetic of every vote the organisation took. Numbers that had been fixed for decades shifted, so the assembly's balance of power moved further towards the states of the newly independent world, and the organisation's committees acquired a large body of new members with their own priorities. Those priorities were practical rather than ideological: development, debt, trade and the status of the territories that had not yet become independent. The rush therefore did not simply enlarge the membership; it redirected the organisation's work for decades to come.

questions.explanation: Seventeen new members shifted the arithmetic of every vote and redirected the organisation's work towards development and decolonisation. The membership grew, but so did the agenda.
questions.hint: Think about what counts in a vote.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A circular that set the timetable
questions.learningObjective: Identify the most controversial feature of the published arrangement.

stimulus.body: A devolution note records that the announcement of self-government named the powers that would be handed over immediately, those reserved to the colonial authority for a stated period, and those which would be transferred only at independence. It also records that the divisions were published in a single table and were the subject of no negotiation at the time of issue.

questions.stem: The planner's memorandum on the circular states that the arrangement's most controversial feature was what?

options.text: The promise of full independence at a date not yet fixed by the announcement.
The restriction that the local assembly could not sit in the capital city.
The absence of any date for the final transfer of authority.
The reservation of certain powers to the colonial authority for a fixed period.

questions.explanation: The note's table reserves named powers to the colonial authority for a stated period, which made the schedule controversial rather than reassuring. The other features either appear in the note or contradict it.
questions.hint: Look at the third column of the published table.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Borders drawn before a colony existed
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the first partition's lines were chosen as they were.

stimulus.body: A legacy note records that when the region was divided by outsiders, the lines chosen were those most convenient for the powers concerned rather than those that would have placed each contested stretch with the community that used it, and that after independence those lines continued to be described in law as the frontiers of the new states.

questions.stem: The memorandum's comparison of the rival partitions shows that the first partition's lines were chosen for what reason?

options.text: The convenience of the powers making the claims, rather than the claims of the communities crossed.
The wishes of the communities crossed by the lines, as reported at the time.
The interests of the future states, whose frontiers were already being planned.
The distances from the coast, to keep the territories dependent on shipping.

questions.explanation: The note says the lines were chosen for the convenience of the powers making the claims, with the communities crossed having no part in the choice. The other reasons appear nowhere in it.
questions.hint: Look at who the note names as the beneficiary.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The contest for the centre
questions.learningObjective: Explain what the contest for the centre revealed about the world order.
questions.stem: The city file's closing note on the centre states that the contest over the central state showed what about the wider world order?

options.text: That the organisation could impose its decisions on any state that resisted them.
That the organisation had been designed to end the rivalry between the great powers.
options.misconception: claims the organisation ended the rivalry

options.text: That the organisation's machinery could not settle a dispute without the rival powers acting inside it.
That the organisation had been rendered ineffective by the conduct of its own members.

questions.explanation: The contest showed the organisation's action depended on great-power agreement, since a force could be authorised only if one of them did not object. The crisis exposed that dependence, not the body's ineffectiveness.
questions.hint: Ask what had to happen before troops could move.
